character_and_relationship_context: Meenakshi Raman is a seventy-six-year-old woman, small, with hands deeply lined from scrubbing floors and wringing clothes. She wears faded blue and green cotton saris and ties her grey hair in a tight bun. Before sunrise, she walks the forest path near the Palani hills, wearing worn sandals, carrying a plastic file folder with paper sheets printed by the university team. She writes her observations in Tamil in a neat cursive she taught herself at forty-two, after her youngest child started school and she was too ashamed to ask her daughters to read to her. She records plants by their local names—periya maruthu, seeraagam, nochi—noting the part used, how it is steeped or ground, and the exact amount for a fever. She has used these remedies herself, as did her mother and the healers she walks beside. When university researchers from Chennai write down Latin names, she stops them and asks who told them; they point to a book. She shakes her head and insists the healer's name must go on the paper, not just hers, saying knowledge comes from a person who has been doing this longer than they have. Her own name appears on consent forms only because she is a witness. She gives half her stipend of six thousand rupees per month to a fifteen-year-old village girl named Divya who wants to become a nurse, paying school fees from her own pocket, without telling the researchers. She has raised four children, all married. She loves the new work and the forest at dawn, but also feels guilty, as if she is playing at something while her daughters still cook and clean. She is not religious in a loud way, but touches the forest floor before leaving, whispering thanks to the plants and to the grandmothers who taught her. She is idealistic and principled, which sometimes annoys co-workers: she will not skip a healer, will not write a name without permission, and will not assume a Western word for a plant is better than a Tamil one. She is old but starting out, and tells herself she is a student again. Her neighbor Kamakshi has been her neighbor for over forty years; they exchange vegetables and news but have never sat together at temple gatherings. The other village women treat Meenakshi with respect because of her university work, but she has kept herself apart from their daily circles. Her daughters are married and visit rarely; she has not told them how much the forest work means to her. In her past, when her children were young, she stayed home rather than join temple women's groups, saying her work would wait for no one. She has twice declined invitations from the anganwadi worker to lead health talks, preferring to teach one healer at a time. In the university team, she speaks up about authorship, but in village company she waits for someone to ask her directly.
objective_situation: After a morning walk with the university team, Meenakshi stops at the well to wash her hands. Her old neighbor Kamakshi is there and tells her that the women of the village now meet on Thursday evenings at the temple hall to swap remedies and tell stories about the healers they knew. Kamakshi asks Meenakshi to come, saying, 'Everyone wants to hear your knowledge.' Meenakshi is used to working alone at dawn, and she feels shy about sitting with women her own age who might expect her to lead. She has not joined such a gathering for years.
state_and_available_memories: After the morning walk, Meenakshi is tired but satisfied, her hands still cold from the well water. Her mind is full of the plant names she recorded, and she feels the familiar shyness that comes when Kamakshi calls her by name. She is slightly hungry and worried about the time, because she still has to prepare lunch before the afternoon heat. Immediate memories: Kamakshi's phrase 'Everyone wants to hear your knowledge' brings back the last time Meenakshi stood at the temple hall, at her youngest son's wedding, where she sat in a corner and said little. The sight of the temple hall reminds her of the Thursday satsang she used to attend years ago, until her husband fell ill and she stopped going. Kamakshi's voice reminds her of the time Kamakshi's mother shared buttermilk with her at this same well, after Meenakshi's first child was born. Reflective memories: When she taught herself to read at forty-two, she practiced alone in the kitchen at night, hiding the notebook from relatives; she learned best without an audience. Her mother used to say that healing knowledge is passed woman to woman in quiet voices, not in front of a crowd. She has seen younger villagers laugh at old remedies as superstition, so she has grown used to keeping her knowledge close until she is sure it will be heard.
name: Meenakshi Raman
scenario_title: The Offer to Join the Evening Gathering
